name: Coconut oil toothpaste
lead: Coconut oil toothpaste is a category of homemade or commercially sold "natural" tooth cleaner in which coconut oil is a principal ingredient, usually mixed with baking soda or similar powders. It is promoted in online looksmaxxing and wellness circles as a gentler, additive-free way to clean and whiten teeth.

Coconut oil is more commonly discussed in connection with oil pulling, an Ayurvedic practice of swishing oil in the mouth, which the American Dental Association has said lacks reliable supporting studies for oral hygiene benefits.[2] Whitening from toothpaste in general works largely through abrasion of surface stain, not by changing the underlying colour of the tooth.[1]
No clinical trial of a coconut-oil-based toothpaste for tooth whitening appears in the sources reviewed for this article.
infobox: Coconut oil, often with baking soda
Sold as cosmetic or homemade; no whitening claim reviewed

paras: Coconut oil pastes are typically described as an oil base blended with a mild abrasive such as baking soda. Commercial versions and home recipes both circulate. Herbal or natural toothpastes in general are marketed to people who wish to avoid artificial ingredients and often omit fluoride and sodium lauryl sulfate.[1]

Abrasion is the main mechanism by which toothpastes remove surface stain, and ordinary toothpastes do this as well as whitening ones. Whitening toothpaste cannot change the natural colour of teeth or reverse discolouration originating inside the tooth.[1] Baking soda is described as a low-abrasive option with no adverse effects reported in clinical studies.[3] Coconut oil itself is not a recognised abrasive or bleaching agent in the sources reviewed.

Oil pulling, in which coconut or other oils are swished in the mouth, is described as an Ayurvedic practice. A 2016 systematic review of randomised trials found the included studies few and too small to be reliable.[2] The American Dental Association says no reliable studies support oral hygiene benefits, and the Canadian Dental Association said in 2014 that it doubted harm but was not convinced of particular benefits.[2] Critics of the practice cited on Wikipedia argue any effect would come from mechanical swishing.[2]

Fluoride toothpaste at 1,000 ppm or more is associated with fewer cavities in children and adolescents in a systematic review, and a 2019 Cochrane review found concentrations below 1,000 ppm unlikely to prevent decay.[1][4] Coconut oil pastes that omit fluoride therefore differ from fluoride products in this respect. Abrasive pastes with a high relative dentin abrasivity are listed among factors in tooth abrasion.[5]

card.summary: Coconut-oil-and-baking-soda tooth paste sold as a gentle natural whitener; no trial shows it whitens.
card.note: Usually fluoride-free; whitening relies on mild abrasion at best.

quick.overview:
Coconut oil toothpaste is a natural or homemade paste built around coconut oil, often with baking soda. It is promoted as an additive-free way to clean and whiten teeth.

No published trial of coconut-oil toothpaste for whitening was found. Related research on oil pulling is described as low quality, and the American Dental Association says reliable studies are lacking.
quick.mechanism: Toothpaste whitening works mainly by abrasively removing surface stain; it does not change the intrinsic colour of the tooth. Coconut oil is not an established abrasive or bleaching agent, so any effect would come from added abrasives such as baking soda.
quick.risks: Most such pastes omit fluoride, which a 2019 Cochrane review links to caries prevention at 1,000 ppm and above. Highly abrasive pastes are listed among causes of tooth abrasion. Risks of the oil itself have not been formally studied.
